 adaptation
 positively
 generalizes
 to
 the
 last
 visuomotor
 adaptation.
Scores
 greater
 than
 1
 indicate
 negative
 transfer
 (interference),
 while
 1
 represents
equivalent
 performance
 at
 transfer
 and
 learning.
2.3.
 MRI
 data
 analysis
2.3.1.
 fMRI
 data
The
 ﬁrst
 three
 volumes
 per
 run
 were
 discarded
 to
 allow
 for
 signal
 equilibra-
tion.
 High-pass
 ﬁltering
 was
 used
 to
 remove
 low-frequency
 drift.
 Motion
 correction
was
 performed
 using
 MCFLIRT
 and
 the
 Brain
 Extraction
 Tool
 (BET)
 was
 used
 to
 strip
the
 skull
 from
 images
 (using
 FSL
 toolboxes,
 http://www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl).
 Statis-
tical
 Parametric
 Mapping
 version
 5
 (SPM5)
 was
 used
 for
 subsequent
 analyses.
 A
mean
 functional
 image
 was
 created
 for
 each
 participant.
 All
 functional
 and
 struc-
tural
 images
 were
 aligned
 to
 this
 functional
 mean
 image.
 The
 Montreal
 Neurological
Institute
 (MNI)
 template
 was
 used
 for
 spatial
 normalization
 [25].
 The
 structural
image
 was
 normalized
 to
 MNI
 space
 ﬁrst
 and
 the
 resulting
 parameters
 were
 applied
to
 the
 functional
 images.
 Functional
 images
 were
 spatially
 smoothed
 using
 a
 full
width
 at
 half-maximum
 8
 mm Gaussian
 smoothing
 kernel.
 Four
 participants
 were
removed
 from
 the
 fMRI
 analyses
 due
 to
 poor
 co-registration
 (leaving
 testing
 order
1:9
 young
 and
 older
 adults;
 testing
 order
 2:8
 young
 and
 7
 older
 adults).
 Boxcar
models
 synchronized
 to
 the
 effect
 of
 interest
 and
 convolved
 with
 an
 estimate
 of
the
 hemodynamic
 response
 function
 were
 used
 for
 statistical
 analyses.
 A
 general
linear
 model
 analysis
 was
 ﬁrst
 conducted
 at
 an
 individual
 level
 for
 motor
 learning
(run
 3)
 and
 motor
 transfer
 (run
 13)
 contrasting
 periods
 of
 movement
 with
 rest.
 Sec-
ond
 level
 random
 effects
 analyses
 were
 run
 for
 single
 group
 whole
 brain
 contrasts
(uncorrected
 p
 =
 .001).
 Imaging
 data
 for
 older
 adults
 in
 orders
 1
 and
 2
 were
 com-
bined
 to
 increase
 power
 as
 they
 demonstrated
 similar
 behavior.
 Similarly,
 young
adults
 in
 orders
 1
 and
 2
 were
 also
 combined
 (see
 ref.
 [11]
 for
 justiﬁcation
 of
 this
approach).
 Contrasts
 identiﬁed
 regions
 of
 greater
 or
 less
 activation
 during
 motor
learning
 versus
 transfer
 for
 both
 young
 and
 older
 adults.
 To
 identify
 regions
 involved
in
 both
 spatial
 working
 memory
 and
 visuomotor
 adaptation,
 masks
 of
 spatial
 work-
ing
 memory
 activation
 established
 with
 separate
 cohorts
 of
 young
 and
 older
 adults
in
 our
 previous
 studies
 [12,16]
 were
 applied
 to
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 activa-
tion
 for
 both
 learning
 and
 transfer.
 Applying
 the
 mask,
 within-group
 analyses
 were
used
 to
 identify
 regions
 where
 activation
 was
 greater
 at
 motor
 learning
 compared
 to
transfer
 and
 vice
 versa
 (uncorrected
 p
 <
 .001).
 Between
 group
 analyses
 distinguished
regions
 in
 which
 young
 or
 older
 adults
 demonstrated
 greater
 or
 less
 activation
 dur-
ing
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer
 (uncorrected
 p
 < .001).
 The
 Talairach
 atlas
 [26]
 was
used
 to
 localize
 signiﬁcant
 areas
 of
 activation.
2.4.
 Statistical
 analyses
 analyses
 were
 conducted
 in
 SPSS.
 Independent
 t-tests
 (using
 the
 mean
of
Statistical
 trials
 for
 each
 participant)
 were
 used
 to
 assess
 differences
 between
 age
 groups
and
 transfer
 orders
 for
 the
 second
 baseline
 run
 (the
 ﬁrst
 run
 was
 treated
 as
 practice
and
 not
 included
 in
 statistical
 analyses).
 Levene’s
 test
 for
 equality
 of
 variances
 was
conducted
 and
 corrected
 t-tests
 were
 used
 if
 equal
 variances
 were
 not
 assumed.
To
 ensure
 that
 participants
 had
 returned
 to
 baseline
 levels
 of
 performance
 (run
 2)
between
 each
 set
 of
 adaptation
 runs,
 the
 last
 4
 trials
 of
 the
 baseline
 run
 immediately
preceding
 the
 last
 adaptation
 run
 (run
 12)
 were
 compared
 to
 the
 last
 4
 trials
 of
run
 2
 using
 a
 paired
 t-test.
 We compared
 performance
 at
 learning
 to
 performance
during
 transfer
 for
 the
 30◦and
 45◦visual
 rotations
 using
 a
 linear
 mixed
 model
 design
with
 a
 compound
 symmetric
 residual
 covariance
 structure.
 Age
 group,
 presentation
order
 and
 trial
 were
 treated
 as
 ﬁxed
 effects,
 and
 all
 2-
 and
 3-way
 interaction
 terms
were
 considered.
 Correlation
 analyses
 were
 used
 to
 assess
 the
 relationship
 between
motor
 learning,
 transfer,
 neuropsychological
 test
 performance
 and
 spatial
 working
memory
 task
 performance.
 Scores
 that
 were
 greater
 than
 2.5
 standard
 deviations
outside
 of
 the
 mean
 were
 considered
 as
 outliers
 and
 removed
 from
 the
 analysis.
3.
 Results
3.1.
 Visuomotor
 adaptation
 task
 performance
At
 baseline
 (run
 2),
 young
 adults
 performed
 better
 than
 older
adults
 in
 terms
 of
 RT
 and
 IEE
 (p
 <
 .01);
 there
 was
 no
 differ-
ence
 between
 groups
 in
 DE
 (t
 =
 .98,
 df
 =
 34,
 p
 =
 .34,
 supplemental
materials
 Table
 S2). The
 two
 testing
 order
 groups
 within
 young
and
 older
 adults
 performed
 similarly
 on
 RT,
 DE
 and
 IEE
 at
 baseline
(p
 >
 .10).
To
 determine
 whether
 baseline
 performance
 was
 similar
 prior
to
 the
 ﬁrst
 and
 last
 visuomotor
 adaptations,
 the
 last
 four
 trials
 of
runs
 2
 and
 12
 were
 compared.
 Young
 adults
 in
 orders
 1
 and
 2
returned
 to
 baseline
 performance
 for
 all
 variables
 (p
 >
 .10
 between
runs
 2
 and
 12),
 indicating
 that
 the
 ﬁrst
 and
 last
 adaptive
 experi-
ences
 had
 similar
 starting
 points.
 Older
 adults
 in
 order
 1
 and
 2
 did
not
 return
 to
 baseline
 in
 terms
 of
 RT
 (t
 =
 2.68,
 df
 =
 8,
 p
 =
 .03,
 t
 =
 4.13,
 =
 8,
 p
 <
 .01).
 Older
 adults
 in
 order
 2
 also
 failed
 to
 return
 to
 base-
line
 in
 terms
 of
 DE
 (t
 =
 3.70,
 df
 =
 8,
 p
 =
 .01).
 We corrected
 for
 this
by
 subtracting
 the
 baseline
 DE
 from
 adaptation
 runs
 to
 account
 for
older
 adults
 not
 returning
 to
 baseline
 levels.
 Statistical
 analyses
 to
identify
 age
 differences
 in
 learning
 and
 transfer
 were
 run
 on
 both
the
 original
 and
 the
 baseline-corrected
 data.
 Since
 there
 was
 no
difference
 in
 the
 pattern
 of
 age,
 learning,
 or
 transfer
 effects,
 data
without
 baseline
 correction
 are
 reported
 for
 both
 young
 and
 older
adults
 for
 ease
 of
 interpretation.
To
 examine
 transfer
 of
 motor
 learning,
 we evaluated
 differences
in
 performance
 during
 the
 ﬁrst
 and
 last
 exposures
 to
 a
 visual
 rota-
tion.
 Analogous
 to
 our
 previous
 work,
 experience
 with
 a
 visuomotor
adaptation
 was
 beneﬁcial
 to
 subsequent
 performance
 [10]. Bene-
ﬁts
 were
 most
 consistently
 found
 for
 both
 the
 30◦and
 45◦visual
rotations
 when
 comparing
 initial
 learning
 (run
 3)
 to
 initial
 trans-
fer
 (run
 13).
 That
 is,
 transfer
 beneﬁts
 diminished
 with
 additional
task
 practice.
 Thus,
 the
 following
 behavioral
 and
 imaging
 statistics
reported
 are
 based
 on
 the
 initial
 learning
 and
 transfer
 runs
 (runs
 3
and
 13,
 respectively).
df
3.2.
 Amount
 of
 learning
Older
 
adults
 
demonstrated
 
a
 
lower
 
amount
 
of
 
learning
compared
 to
 young
 adults
 (mean
 learning
 percentages
 across
 con-
ditions
 for
 older
 adults
 ranged
 from
 9
 to
 27%
 and
 for
 young
 adults
33
 to
 64%,
 DE
 (t
 =
 2.4,
 df
 =
 33,
 p
 =
 .02),
 IEE
 (t
 =
 2.30,
 df
 =
 34,
 p
 =
 .03).
It
 is
 notable
 that,
 although
 older
 adults
 demonstrated
 less
 learning
than
 young
 adults,
 they
 exhibited
 equivalent,
 or
 even
 greater,
 sav-
ings
 at
 transfer
 of
 learning
 on
 some
 of
 the
 performance
 variables
(see
 below).
 Thus
 it
 appears
 that
 the
 magnitude
 of
 learning
 that
occurred
 did
 not
 directly
 inﬂuence
 transfer
 performance.
3.3.
 Transfer
 to
 30◦visuomotor
 adaptation
Young
 and
 older
 adults
 demonstrated
 reduced
 DE
 at
 transfer
 to
the
 30◦rotation
 compared
 to
 initial
 learning
 to
 the
 same
 extent
(Fig.
 1A
 and
 B,
 main
 effect
 for
 presentation
 order,
 F(1,32.20) =
 5.83,
p
 =
 .02).
 Similarly,
 both
 groups
 decreased
 IEE
 at
 motor
 transfer
(Fig.
 1C
 and
 D,
 main
 effect
 for
 presentation
 order,
 F(1,31.56) =
 3.35,
p
 <
 .01).
 However,
 young
 adults
 demonstrated
 greater
 transfer
 for
IEE
 than
 older
 adults
 (age
 group
 ×
 presentation
 order
 interaction,
F(1,31.56) =
 3.98,
 p
 =
 .05).
 RT
 was
 similar
 for
 both
 groups
 and
 did
 not
change
 at
 transfer
 compared
 to
 initial
 learning
 (Fig.
 1E
 and
 F).
3.4.
 Transfer
 to
 45◦visuomotor
 adaptation
Older
 adults
 demonstrated
 a
 larger
 beneﬁt
 from
 prior
 training
compared
 to
 young
 adults
 in
 terms
 of
 reducing
 DE
 at
 motor
 trans-
fer
 to
 the
 45◦rotation
 (Fig.
 2A
 and
 B,
 age
 group
 ×
 presentation
order
 interaction,
 F(1,32.12) =
 3.88,
 p
 =
 .05).
 Overall,
 young
 adults
demonstrated
 smaller
 IEE
 than
 older
 adults
 (main
 effect
 for
 age,
F(1,31.87) =
 13.99,
 p
 <
 .01).
 Neither
 group
 demonstrated
 a
 change
 in
IEE
 at
 transfer
 with
 respect
 to
 initial
 learning
 (Fig.
 2C
 and
 D;
 no
 sig-
niﬁcant
 main
 effect
 or
 interactions
 with
 presentation
 order).
 There
was
 a
 trend
 for
 RT
 to
 diminish
 at
 transfer
 (Fig.
 2E
 and
 F,
 main
 effect
for
 presentation
 order,
 F(1,31.93) =
 2.98,
 p
 =
 .09).
3.5.
 Spatial
 working
 memory
 contributions
 to
 motor
 learning
 and
transfer
Young
 adults
 performed
 better
 on
 the
 spatial
 working
 memory
assessments
 than
 the
 older
 adults
 (p
 <
 .05:
 card
 rotation,
 forward
and
 backward
 Corsi
 blocks
 (see
 supplemental
 materials
 Table
 S3).
To
 better
 understand
 the
 contributions
 of
 spatial
 working
 memory
to
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer,
 we examined
 correlations
 between
performance
 on
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 task
 during
 runs
 3
 and
